story_ideas.title: States' Use of Program Integrity Tools in Medicaid Home Care
story_ideas.headline: The state is watching your home aide's hours more closely than it used to

story_ideas.summary: Oct 5, 2026 Issue Brief This issue brief provides new information about Medicaid home care program's use of program integrity tools from KFF’s most recent survey of state Medicaid home care programs.
story_ideas.consumer: If your Medicaid home care hours are verified electronically, ask your state agency what happens to your services when a visit fails to record, and keep your own log of who came and when.
story_ideas.b2b: Home care agencies need to know which integrity tools their state has adopted before an audit reaches payroll, because the compliance cost lands on the same margin that pays aides.

story_ideas.headline: Your doctor's practice joined a hospital system. The quality gain was modest.

story_ideas.hook: RAND examined exactly the consolidation older patients have been living through, and the word it reached for was modest.

trends_raw: Volume barely moved, 160 evidence candidates against 158 on 10/04/26, with 11 first surfaced in this run. What changed is where the new material sits. Medicare and Medicaid gained five items and is now 41 items from 9 sources, still at 0.051 cohesion, which means it is the busiest beat and not a subject; housing and financial security each lost one. The genuinely new evidence is institutional rather than governmental: two KFF briefs from the same state Medicaid home care survey published 10/05/26, two RAND reports the same day, the FTC letters to 24 companies, and a 10/05/26 Federal Register correction to the 08/13/26 APM payment advisory. That is a different shape from the last three runs, which were carried by Federal Register fee notices and BLS prints. The BLS series have not moved at all: the newest workforce and assisted living items are 34 days old, the September employment prints are the same September prints pitched on 10/02/26, and the August earnings figures are the same August figures. Long-term care remains the only cluster that actually coheres, at 0.114 with 8 items, and monitored publishers have matched 4 of them, so it is the one beat where we are not first. Fifty-five confirmed gaps stand against 76 items on beats no monitored publisher covers. Two things have now gone several runs without being pitched in their own right: the American Community Survey 2023 state aging and housing profile, which has supplied supporting evidence since 09/25/26 and carries the only state-level population figures in the file, and the Senior Medicare Patrol supplement from 09/10/26, which is the only item in the corpus aimed at helping an individual beneficiary dispute a bill.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Medicare and Medicaid was the busiest beat in this run, 41 items from 9 sources, and it is not one story: those items share a tag, not a subject. One thread inside it is worth pulling out whole. On 10/05/26 the Federal Trade Commission sent letters to 24 of the nation's largest healthcare services companies reminding them of the legal obligation to give patients timely, accurate and complete pricing information, and that failing to do so can be an unfair or deceptive practice. The same day, RAND published an analysis of Medicare Severity Diagnosis Related Group upcoding in California hospitals between 2018 and 2023, finding upcoding increased payments for commercial stays and raised out-of-pocket costs for some Medicare Advantage patients. One document is about what a patient is told before care. The other is about what the chart says afterward. On 10/02/26 the FTC, with the Utah and Nevada attorneys general, sued a contact lens retailer over advertised prices that were not the prices charged.

**Why it matters:** The RAND finding is the stake, not the letters. How a stay is coded is chosen by nobody the patient can see, is not printed on anything a patient receives, and according to that report moved what some Medicare Advantage enrollees paid out of pocket. Twenty-four companies have now been told in writing what they owe patients on price; no record in this run gives a patient the other half, a way to check the code assigned to their own stay against the care delivered. Medical care prices by the BLS Consumer Price Index stood at 593 (1982-84=100) in August 2026, up 1.6% year over year, which is the backdrop and not the explanation for an individual bill moving.

**Why pitch this now:** The FTC letters and both RAND reports published 10/05/26 and were first collected in this run; the Lens.com complaint is dated 10/02/26. **Angle:** Whether an older patient can establish what their hospital stay was coded as, and what that code did to their share of the bill, at a moment when federal enforcement is aimed at what companies disclose rather than at what they record. Working title: "The Price You Were Quoted and the Code You Were Billed." For Medicare and Medicare Advantage enrollees who have had an inpatient stay in the past year, and the adult children who open the statements.
